extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy; those studying Hobbes' Leviathan
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts Hobbesian principles governing the creation, definition, rights, and limits of a commonwealth and sovereign authority (chapters on generation of commonwealth, rights of sovereigns, and kinds of commonwealth). Useful for interpreting or applying Hobbes' theory of sovereignty and civil peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generation of a Common-wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: The only way to erect a Common Power able to defend people and secure them to peace and industry is to confer all their power and strength upon one Man, or upon one Assembly of men, that may reduce all their Wills, by plurality of voices, unto one Will — i.e., appoint one person or assembly to bear their person and authorise all his actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Full authorization (each man authorises and gives up his right of governing himself to the chosen representative) is more than mere consent; it is a real unity in one person by covenant of every man with every man. This conferral creates a body (COMMON-WEALTH/CIVITAS) whose delegated strength, by terror of that power, can form the wills of all to peace and common defence. Example phrasing from text: 'I Authorise and give up my Right of Governing my selfe, to this Man, or to this Assembly of men…'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a Common-wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: A Common-wealth is 'One Person, of whose Acts a great Multitude, by mutuall Covenants one with another, have made themselves every one the Author, to the end he may use the strength and means of them all, as he shall think expedient, for their Peace and Common Defence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition locates the essence of the commonwealth in the person (or representative) who acts on behalf of the united multitude; the commonwealth's legitimacy and function derive from that representative exercising the collectively-authorised power for peace and defence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign and subject — modes of attainment
rubrics_metrics.description: Sovereign power (the Person who bears the commonwealth) is attained either by natural force (violence, conquest, parental domination) or by voluntary agreement (men agreeing to submit to a man or assembly for protection). The latter is a 'political common-wealth' or 'common-wealth by institution.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes voluntary institution from acquisition by force; the following rights and obligations Hobbes discusses are primarily tied to commonwealths instituted by covenant, though he treats both kinds as sources of sovereignty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjects cannot lawfully change the form of government
rubrics_metrics.description: Because subjects have covenanted one with another to own and be author of all actions of the sovereign, they cannot lawfully make a new covenant to obey another or depose their sovereign without his permission; doing so would break their covenant and be unjust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deposing a sovereign would take from him what is his own (his conferred sovereignty) and thus be injustice. The text argues that returning to a disunited multitude undermines the peace the covenant sought to achieve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign power cannot be forfeited by the sovereign
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the right to bear the person of them all was given to the sovereign by covenant of subjects with one another (not by covenant of the sovereign to subjects), there can be no breach of covenant on the sovereign’s part that frees subjects from subjection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes argues that covenants are powerless without the public sword; the sovereign makes no prior covenant with subjects, and attempts to adjudicate breach of sovereign covenant would return to force. Therefore forfeiture claims are invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dissent after a majoritarian institution is not protected
rubrics_metrics.description: If the major part of an assembly has declared a sovereign, those who dissented must now consent and be taken to authorise the sovereign’s actions; protestation by a dissenter is contrary to the covenant and may justify their punishment or destruction as reverting to the pre-covenant state of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entry to the original congregation implies tacit covenant to stand by majority decrees. Hobbes frames dissenters who refuse to submit as reverting to the state of war and thereby vulnerable to enforcement by others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjects cannot justly accuse the sovereign of injustice
rubrics_metrics.description: Because each subject is by institution an author of all the sovereign’s actions and judgments, whatever the sovereign does cannot be, properly speaking, an injury to any subject; a subject who complains thereby complains of an act of which he himself is author.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes separates 'iniquity' from 'injustice': sovereigns may do iniquitous things (morally bad) but not injustice (breach of the civil covenant) in the proper legal sense, because subjects authorised those acts when instituting the sovereign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign is unpunishable by subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Consequent to subjects being the authors of sovereign actions, no subject can justly kill or punish the sovereign, for that would amount to punishing oneself for one’s own acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punishment by subjects for sovereign acts is illegitimate; judicial or coercive remedies against the sovereign by subjects are precluded by the foundational covenant logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign judges what is necessary for peace and defence
rubrics_metrics.description: The sovereign, entrusted with the end of peace and defence, has the right to judge both the means necessary for those ends and the hindrances or disturbances to them, and may do whatever he deems necessary beforehand (prevention) or afterward (recovery) to preserve peace and security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because right to the end implies right to the means, sovereign discretion over preventative and remedial measures is justified. This is a principle for allocation of competence, not a check on how the sovereign exercises that competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign determines what doctrines are fit to be taught
rubrics_metrics.description: The sovereign has authority to judge which opinions and doctrines are conducive to peace and which are averse, to decide who may speak to multitudes, and who shall examine books before publication, because opinions produce actions and regulating opinions serves peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes allows doctrinal regulation for reasons of public order: teaching of truths may be regulated where their free propagation would threaten peace. He also acknowledges tension with truth but subsumes doctrine regulation under the aim of preserving concord.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign prescribes rules of property (proprietie) and civil law
rubrics_metrics.description: It belongs to sovereignty to prescribe the rules by which every man may know what goods he may enjoy and what actions he may do without being molested by other subjects — i.e., to establish property, rights (meum et tuum), and civil laws particular to each commonwealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Property rules are necessary to avoid the pre-constitutional right to all things that causes war; these rules are authoritative acts of the sovereign in service of public peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign has the right of judicature (decision of controversies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Annexed to sovereignty is the right to hear and decide all controversies — about civil or natural law, or about fact — because without judicial decision there is no protection of one subject against another and law is in vain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicature is essential to prevent regression to private self-protection (state of war); therefore sovereign control of courts and adjudication is a core sovereign competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign makes war, peace, and levies resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Sovereign has the right to make war and peace with other nations, judge when these are for the public good, assemble and command forces, and levy money upon subjects to defray expenses of defence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Military command and fiscal authority are necessary because the people's defence depends on armies and the union of strength under one command; command of militia is a mark of sovereignty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign chooses counsellors, ministers, magistrates, and officers
rubrics_metrics.description: Sovereignty includes the right to appoint all counsellors and ministers, both in peace and war, because the sovereign is charged with the end of public peace and defence and may use such means as he thinks fit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appointment power is justified instrumentally: sovereign chooses agents to carry out those ends; delegation is permitted but remains under sovereign discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign may reward and punish (and arbitrate when no law exists)
rubrics_metrics.description: The sovereign is entrusted with the power of rewarding with riches or honour and of punishing with corporal or pecuniary punishments or ignominy according to previously made law; where no law determines the measure, he may act arbitrarily as he judges most conducive to encouraging service or deterring disservice to the commonwealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This grants wide discretionary penal and reward power to the sovereign, constrained only by prior laws when they exist; otherwise sovereign judgment governs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign assigns honour and public order
rubrics_metrics.description: It belongs to the sovereign to create laws of honour and public ranking (titles, orders of place and dignity) and to enforce them, because such regulation prevents emulation, factions, and quarrels that otherwise threaten the commonwealth’s peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes treats honorific and ceremonial regulation as instruments for stabilizing social hierarchies and reducing sources of dispute among ambitious subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sovereign rights are indivisible and incommunicable
rubrics_metrics.description: The rights that constitute sovereignty are essential, inseparable, and incommunicable; dividing them (militia, judicature, taxation, doctrine control) renders the rest ineffective and risks civil war because protection requires their unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes argues that transfer of any sovereign prerogative without renouncing sovereignty itself is void in effect: splitting powers undermines the capacity to secure peace, and historical division of powers produced civil war in England.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grants of prerogatives do not transfer sovereignty without direct renunciation
rubrics_metrics.description: Because these rights are inseparable, if a sovereign appears to grant them away in words but does not directly renounce the sovereign name and authority, the grant is void — sovereignty remains with the grantor unless expressly renounced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partial grants of sovereign functions (money, militias, judicature) leave the sovereign ineffective; only explicit renunciation of sovereignty can transfer the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human motivations justify need for common power (contrast with irrational creatures)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike irrational creatures, humans compare themselves, use reason and speech to magnify or diminish good and evil, contest administration, form factions, and distinguish injury from damage — all of which produce discord; therefore human nature makes necessary an artificial covenant (common power) plus a common authority to keep them in awe and direct actions to common benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is Hobbes’ anthropological justification for instituting commonwealth and investing indivisible power in a sovereign: human passions and speech create instability that only a sovereign can manage.

rubrics_metrics.name: There are only three kinds of commonwealth by institution
rubrics_metrics.description: Because sovereignty must reside in one man, an assembly of all, or an assembly of a part, there are three possible forms of commonwealth by institution: MONARCHY (one), DEMOCRACY or popular commonwealth (assembly of all), and ARISTOCRACY (assembly of a part).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes treats other labels (tyranny, oligarchy, anarchy) as descriptive or pejorative, not as distinct forms; variants like elective or limited kingships are classified by where sovereignty actually resides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordinate representatives are dangerous (no two sovereigns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Erecting subordinate or second general representatives of the same people risks creating two sovereigns and dividing sovereignty, which will divide power and reduce the commonwealth to the condition of war; therefore additional general representation is absurd and dangerous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes warns against multiple overlapping general representatives (e.g., provincial assemblies claiming equal sovereign authority), which would undermine unity and peace; limited delegates for specific ends are permissible only within sovereign limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative criteria for forms: monarchy vs assemblies
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluative criteria for comparing forms include: unity of private and public interest (monarch better unites them); access to counsel (monarch can choose advisers in secrecy), constancy of resolutions (monarch less subject to number-based inconstancy), risk of internal disagreement and faction (assemblies more vulnerable), and dangers like favourites, infant succession, or regents (possible in all forms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hobbes lists functional advantages and disadvantages to judge which form better achieves peace and security in given circumstances; monarchy often preferred for decisive, unified action, while assemblies bring instability from number and faction but share other risks.
